Representing chemical and enzymatic reactions in fingerprint space for applicability filtering and classification
abstract: Abstract Molecular and reaction fingerprints are widely used as static descriptors, but their relationship to graph-level reaction application remains unclear. We address this question in counted Extended-Connectivity Fingerprint (ECFP) space, representing reactions as signed differences between product and substrate fingerprints. We define ECFP-compatible templates, for which graph-level reaction application induces a constant fingerprint displacement, yielding a functorial mapping from graph transformations to affine translations in fingerprint space. We also introduce reaction-center ECFPs to encode the local environments required for template application and to provide a fast coordinate-wise prefilter for graph-level reaction applicability. We evaluate this framework on USPTO-50k and MetaNetX reactions across a range of ECFP radii. Both representations carry predictive information for reaction-class and enzyme-class classification, with reaction-center ECFPs contributing information not captured by reaction ECFPs alone. This framework connects reaction templates and reaction fingerprints to molecular pathway search and reaction-property prediction in fingerprint space.

title: Molecular function-guided unsupervised similarity-based enrichment for low-data virtual screening
abstract: Abstract Identifying bioactive compounds for orphan or understudied protein targets remains a significant hurdle in drug discovery due to the lack of sufficient structure-activity relationship (SAR) data. We present MolFuSE (Molecular Function-guided Similarity Explorer), an unsupervised, projection-based enrichment framework designed for low-data virtual screening and ligand repurposing. MolFuSE leverages manifold learning—specifically uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP)—to create low-dimensional similarity spaces based on a reference set of ligands known to bind proteins with the same molecular function as the target. Through systematic evaluation across nine protein targets and their functional classes, we demonstrate that UMAP embeddings of Mordred 2D descriptors act as a strong “potency filter”, significantly outperforming traditional topological fingerprints in the early enrichment of high-potency inhibitors (<100 nM). While extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFP4) fingerprints achieve superior global ranking (receiver operating characteristic (ROC)-area under the curve (AUC) 0.961 vs. 0.863), the descriptor-based approach provides more robust early recognition (enrichment factor at 1% (EF@1%)) when the reference set itself is small. Crucially, we identify a critical point in data scaling: performance peaks at a reference set size of approximately 10,000 compounds and degrades for larger sets due to descriptor-space dilution from structurally diverse weak binders. MolFuSE provides a computationally efficient, interpretable tool for prioritizing high-affinity candidates when target-specific data is unavailable.

Somatic mutations in neurodegeneration: from detection to disease mechanisms
abstract: Abstract Somatic mutations are postzygotic DNA alterations that accumulate throughout development and aging, underlying somatic mosaicism across cell populations. Neurons are particularly vulnerable due to oxidative stress, high metabolic demand, and age-related decline in DNA damage response pathways, promoting cell-type-specific dysfunction. Somatic repeat instability is an established driver in Huntington’s disease, yet the extent and functional impact of somatic mutagenesis in Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis remains unresolved. This article highlights how advances in single-cell and single-molecule sequencing, integrated with computational and machine learning approaches, support detecting ultra-rare variants and establishing causal links between somatic mutagenesis and neurodegeneration.

Chronic pain-like responses revealed by allodynia and hyperalgesia in the ant Lasius niger
abstract: Abstract Background Allodynia (pain in response to normally non-noxious stimuli) and hyperalgesia (increased sensitivity to painful stimuli) are well-established indicators of pain sensitization after tissue damage in vertebrates. These phenomena may also offer valuable insights into nociceptive processing in invertebrates. We assessed behavioural evidence for allodynia and hyperalgesia following two types of peripheral injury (tarsus amputation or burning) and sham treatment in black garden ants ( Lasius niger , Hymenoptera: Formicidae). At 20 min, 24 h, and 96 h post-anaesthesia, a ramping hot plate assay with sublethal, but increasingly noxious, temperatures was used to assess allodynia and hyperalgesia. Locomotor speed and proportion of time spent moving were quantified to detect increased responsiveness at normally non-noxious temperatures (allodynia) or exaggerated responses at higher temperatures (hyperalgesia). Results We observed an earlier onset of responsiveness in ants with tarsus amputations and burns compared to controls, consistent with allodynia, which was stronger and more consistent in tarsus-amputated ants and at later time points. Evidence for hyperalgesia was limited and time-dependent: amputated ants showed a steeper response increase at higher temperatures at earlier time points, but not at 96 h. Burn-treated ants showed less consistent evidence of allodynia and no evidence of hyperalgesia. Conclusions These findings suggest that sensitization extends beyond the acute injury phase and align with broader evidence for chronic, pain-like processing in insects. As a new injury model in insects, the burn treatment needs to be refined, or the underlying mechanisms may be different to those involved in classic, amputation-induced sensitization.

Selective attention or inattention? Enabling efficient perception in embodied intelligence agents
abstract: Abstract As embodied intelligence increasingly operates in the physical world, perception efficiency, robustness, and adaptability become central bottlenecks separating artificial agents from biological organisms. Unlike conventional perception pipelines, biological perception is inherently selective and resource-aware: attention amplifies task-relevant information, while inattention suppresses distraction and redundancy. This survey investigates attention-driven adaptive perception as a promising mechanism for improving embodied systems. We consolidate interdisciplinary findings from neuroscience, cognitive science, robotics, and machine learning to clarify the distinct yet complementary roles of selective attention and inattention in optimizing perceptual processing. Building on these insights, we introduce the Unified Selective Attention and Inattention Model (U-SAIM) and extend it into a three-tier architectural framework that maps biological principles to embodied perception systems. Guided by this structure, we review existing implementations across robotics, multimodal fusion, lightweight perception, and attention modulation strategies, extracting design patterns and performance implications. Moreover, we discuss the challenges and opportunities for future development. Together, these perspectives chart a unified theoretical and practical roadmap toward attentional embodied perception—agents capable of perceiving, reasoning, and acting with the adaptive intelligence, efficiency, and flexibility that define human perception.

Which is more effective at improving uptake of bowel cancer screening: text message reminders or patient navigation? Results from a three-arm RCT
abstract: Abstract Background Text message reminders (TMRs) and patient navigation (PN) increase bowel cancer screening uptake. To date, no studies have directly compared these interventions with one another. Methods We conducted a three-arm randomised controlled trial with individuals, in London, who had not completed bowel cancer screening within 18 weeks of invitation. Participants were randomised to receive no reminder (usual care), TMRs at 19, 21, 23 and 25 weeks, or a TMR at 19 weeks, with telephone PN at 21, 23 and 25 weeks. The primary outcome was participation within 26 weeks of invitation. Differences were assessed using logistic regression. Results On an intention-to-treat basis ( n = 3129), uptake was higher in the TMR and PN groups, compared with usual care (6.5% vs. 2.0%, p < 0.001; 7.5% vs. 2.0%, p < 0.001). There was no significant difference between TMR and PN groups. In the per-protocol analysis ( n = 2294), uptake was significantly higher in the PN group than the TMR group (8.6 vs. 12.6%, p < 0.025). Subgroup analyses revealed telephone PN was significantly more effective than TMRs for men, specifically (14.5% vs. 6.7%, p < 0.001). Conclusions While TMRs are no more effective than PN in general, implementing PN could help reduce disparities in uptake between men and women. Trial registration ISRCTN17245519.

Reduced attenuation of neural activation during fear extinction learning in patients with anxiety disorders: a delayed fear extinction fMRI study
abstract: Abstract Clarifying the patterns of neural activation during fear extinction in anxiety disorders (ADs) is essential for advancing our understanding of inhibitory learning. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly characterized in large, heterogeneous cohorts of patients. Utilizing a delayed fear extinction fMRI paradigm, this study examined neural responses in 280 patients with ADs — comprising panic disorder, agoraphobia, panic disorder with agoraphobia, social anxiety disorder, and multiple specific phobias — compared to 103 healthy controls (HC). The attenuation of neural activation to conditioned fear (CS+) and safety (CS−) stimuli from early versus late extinction was compared between groups. Subjective ratings of US-expectancy, arousal, and valence were also collected. In a whole-brain voxelwise analysis, patients showed significantly reduced attenuation of neural activation across both CS+ and CS− relative to HC from early compared to late phases of extinction learning. This pattern was observed in a broad network, encompassing the insular cortex (IC) and bilateral supplementary motor area (SMA), among other regions. No interaction between group and stimulus type was observed. Region-of-interest analysis of the left anterior insular cortex confirmed that reduced attenuation in this region represents a robust neural signature of altered extinction learning in ADs. Furthermore, patients reported persistently higher fear expectancy and arousal than HC, consistent with sustained alterations in threat-related processing following extinction training. Together, these findings highlight altered extinction-related neural attenuation as a transdiagnostic feature of ADs, offering novel insights into the neural mechanisms underlying fear extinction.

Impaired outcome-based decision-making in human cocaine addiction
abstract: Abstract Despite rising global rates for cocaine addiction, treatments options are limited. Psychological treatments remain the standard option but have only modest effectiveness. One major barrier to treatment success is that patients often make disadvantageous decisions that go against recovery, highlighting the need for strategies to support decision-making. Converging evidence indicates that decision-making deficits in cocaine addiction are driven by impaired processing of outcomes and risks. We investigated how patients with cocaine addiction use explicit outcomes and risk information to guide decision-making. One-hundred-and-five patients with moderate-to-severe cocaine use disorder (CUD) and 80 healthy control volunteers completed a decision-making task in which reward, loss, and probability information were provided explicitly. A subset of participants underwent diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging to investigate the orbitofronto-striatal white matter tracts that underpin decision-making. We used generalized linear mixed-effects models to determine how rewards, losses, and probability influence decisions, and combined probabilistic tractography with principal component analysis to characterize the white matter tracts. We found that patients incorporated explicit probability information into their decisions to the same degree as control participants but showed reduced integration of outcomes. Notably, patients were less likely to integrate losses into their decisions than rewards. Although orbitofronto-striatal white matter tracts did not differ between groups, individual variability predicted the extent to which reward and loss information guided decisions, irrespective of diagnosis. Overall, these findings reveal fundamental challenges in using outcomes, particularly negative ones, to guide decision-making in patients with CUD, emphasizing the need for additional support to promote adaptive choices during recovery.

title: Defect-tolerant carrier injection in MoS2 enabled by double-sided recessed Ti contacts
abstract: Abstract Contact variability remains a major obstacle for scaled two-dimensional transistors, yet whether electrode contact type can control the defect sensitivity of carrier-injection barriers remains unresolved. Here we show that double-sided recessed Ti contacts strongly stabilise MoS 2 carrier-injection barriers against changes in sulfur-vacancy position. By comparing matched MoS 2 model families based on one-sided top Ti contacts and double-sided recessed Ti contacts under the same ordered sulfur-vacancy sequence, first-principles electronic structure and non-equilibrium transport calculations reveal a clear contact-type dependence. For the near-edge vacancy, the Schottky barrier height (SBH) decreases from 0.58 eV for the one-sided top Ti contact to 0.21 eV for the double-sided recessed Ti contact, while the nominal position-dependent SBH variation is reduced by about 85%. Electron transmission calculations further show that this barrier stabilisation results in higher transmission and lower access energies for propagating channel states. The results identify double-sided recessed Ti contacts as a strategy for reducing sulfur-vacancy-induced barrier variability in Ti–MoS 2 electronics.

title: Enhanced electrocatalytic oxygen reduction to H₂O with high selectivity via 2D 1T-MoS₂ integrated with functionalized carbon nanohorns
abstract: Abstract Developing cost-effective and high-performance electrocatalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) is essential for advancing anion-exchange membrane fuel cell technologies. In this study, we report a robust heterostructure formed by covalently functionalized carbon nanohorns (CNH-N) integrated with metallic 1T-MoS 2 2D nanosheets. Through tailored diazonium chemistry, positively charged ammonium groups were introduced onto CNHs, enabling strong electrostatic and van der Waals interactions with negatively charged exfoliated MoS 2 . Structural and spectroscopic analyses confirm successful functionalization, enhanced defect modulation, and intimate CNH–MoS 2 coupling. The resulting CNH-N-MoS 2 catalyst exhibits remarkable ORR performance, including an optimized onset potential of 0.80 V, reduced charge-transfer resistance, and a dominant four-electron reduction pathway with ~94% selectivity toward H 2 O, which is comparable to commercial Pt/C. These results highlight how controlled chemical functionalization and heterointerface engineering can synergistically enhance catalytic activity and stabilize the 1T-MoS 2 phase. The CNH-N-MoS 2 heterostructures thus represent a promising class of platinum-group-metal-free/low-metal-content electrocatalysts for efficient fuel cell applications.

Cortical α-synuclein pathology induces neuronal hypoactivity and circuit changes but not functional impairments in a model of early Lewy body dementia
abstract: Abstract Posterior cortical impairments in visuospatial/perceptual function are common non-motor symptoms of the Lewy Body Dementias (LBD) and are relatively specific for LBDs compared to other dementias. Across populations, cognitive impairments correlate with the presence of α-synuclein (α-syn) pathology in limbic and neocortical brain regions. However, the specific role that α-syn pathology plays in driving cortical circuit dysfunction and cognitive impairment remains controversial. We hypothesized that inducing α-syn pathology in primary visual cortex (V1) in mice would impair neuronal activity and encoding of visual information, leading to visuoperceptual impairments. To test this, we injected α-syn pre-formed fibrils (PFF) into V1, causing the formation of sparse Lewy-like pathology. Using longitudinal in vivo two-photon (2P) calcium imaging over 6 months, we recorded visually evoked activity of pyramidal cells in layer 2/3 (L2/3) and quantified α-syn pathology using C05-05, a fluorescent ligand that binds aggregated α-syn. Measuring population activity, we found a greater percentage of neurons in PFF-injected mice were responsive to visual stimuli with lower direction selectivity compared to controls at 4–5 months post-injection (MPI). Neurons with somatic Lewy-like inclusions showed reduced activity compared to neighboring neurons without inclusions. Conversely, neurons without somatic inclusions showed increased activity, positively correlated with the local burden of α-syn pathology. Using a coherent motion discrimination task, we found no impairments in visuoperceptual ability in PFF-injected mice. Our results demonstrate that α-syn pathology leads to reductions in neuronal activity in cells with somatic inclusions and reciprocal changes in local population activity but does not impair visuoperceptual function. Reflecting the early stages of neocortical α-syn pathology, our model provides a framework for future studies to better understand the heterogeneity of cognitive symptoms and α-syn pathology across patients.
